name: The Idols
rootCause: The Idols NFT staking contract distributes stETH rewards to both the from and to addresses on every safeTransferFrom call without checking whether sender and receiver are the same address. By calling safeTransferFrom(address(this), address(this), tokenId), an attacker simultaneously claims rewards as both sender and receiver in a single operation without relinquishing the NFT, doubling the reward accumulation rate indefinitely. To bypass any Address.isContract() guard that would block a contract from holding the NFT, the attacker placed the entire exploit loop inside the attack contract's constructor: during construction extcodesize of the deploying address is still zero, causing it to appear as an EOA. The constructor looped 2,000 self-transfers, harvesting double stETH rewards on each iteration, then transferred all accumulated stETH and the NFT back to the attacker before self-destructing. The exploit was repeated approximately 15 times across multiple blocks, draining a total of approximately 97 stETH (~$340K). Vulnerable code snippet: Attack Tx: 0x5e989304b1fb61ea0652db4d0f9476b8882f27191c1f1d2841f8977cb8c5284c Analysis: TheIdolsNFT

descriptions.text: Some reflections are better left unseen. The Idols NFT found out the hard way - never trust a mirror. A flaw in their reward system let an attacker drain 97 stETH ($324k) by setting sender and receiver to the same address.

The Idols NFT staking contract distributes stETH rewards to both the from and to addresses on every safeTransferFrom call without checking whether sender and receiver are the same address. By calling safeTransferFrom(address(this), address(this), tokenId), an attacker simultaneously claims rewards as both sender and receiver in a single operation without relinquishing the NFT, doubling the reward accumulation rate indefinitely. To bypass any Address.isContract() guard that would block a contract from holding the NFT, the attacker placed the entire exploit loop inside the attack contract's constructor: during construction extcodesize of the deploying address is still zero, causing it to appear as an EOA. The constructor looped 2,000 self-transfers, harvesting double stETH rewards on each iteration, then transferred all accumulated stETH and the NFT back to the attacker before self-destructing. The exploit was repeated approximately 15 times across multiple blocks, draining a total of approximately 97 stETH (~$340K). The attacker exploited a vulnerability in The Idols project's smart contract to steal 97 stETH (approximately $324,000) from the project.

On January 14, 2025, The Idols NFT staking contract on Ethereum was exploited through repeated NFT self-transfers, resulting in the loss of about 97 stETH (≈$340,000). The attacker abused reward logic to repeatedly reset and claim staking rewards without moving the token. The protocol's reward logic allowed self-transfers of NFTs, and the _beforeTokenTransfer function deleted and reset claimedSnapshots when sender and receiver were the same and balance was one. This error enabled infinite reward claims through repeated self-transfers.

An attacker noticed a vulnerability in a smart contract for The Idols, an NFT project that also incorporates ETH staking functionality. They discovered that a function used to distribute rewards had a bug when the sender and recipient addresses were the same, allowing a holder to repeatedly claim rewards. By taking advantage of this bug, they were able to siphon 97 stETH (~$324,000) from the project. Although The Idols boasts of two audits from several years ago, the contract containing the vulnerability may not have been audited.
